Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. Our approach also offers a flexible framework for exploring different network architectures and providing meaningful comparisons between models with varying parameters. We've open-sourced our code and results to guide future TCN-related research. 

We've successfully applied our method to 10 signal-level and 10 waveform-level classification datasets, yielding state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results across 9 datasets, significantly outperforming the current state-of-the-art TCN benchmark by a margin of 6.98% on average across these 9 datasets. Moreover, our approach has been found to be robust in low-data scenarios, delivering consistent improvements across 7 datasets with a data reduction ratio of 10x.

Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation and contrast it with existing data repair approaches. Moreover, we have developed an implementation of our approach in SquirreL, an open-source, third-generation Java-based database management system capable of handling complex data sources. Experimental evaluations have been conducted using real-world datasets, showcasing the efficacy of our approach. Finally, we identify potential directions for further research, such as exploring the computational complexity of various data repair scenarios and extending our four-valued truth theory to handle additional types of dependencies. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The code is available at https://github.com/zwang84/end-to-end-monocular-pose-network.git. The project has been presented at the IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV) workshop of the special interest group on "3D Human Sensing" in 2019.

This often misplaced trust is the foundation on which our objective is built – namely to minimize the reliance on device hardware and software components for users to withstand cyber threats. 

We introduce an innovative multi-domain hardware setup consisting of isolated sections, where programs are partitioned statically to prevent malicious interaction. 

A few key hardware components with proven security functionality are integrated to grant secure temporary access to processing resources and external input/output interfaces simultaneously.

To manage these hardware components, we introduce OctopOS, a unique OS comprising several secure subsystems working together in distrust. 

We showcase a functioning prototype, incorporating our hardware and software, utilizing a combined CPU-FPGA board with an acceptable additional hardware expense in comparison to existing SoCs. 

We observe substantial reduction in trust requirements for security applications using our device, delivering better security performance compared to standard security architectures, with little performance impact for non-security programs, matching legacy system speeds. 

We illustrate the versatility of our design by implementing multiple hardware configurations and adapting the entire system to accommodate these variations. 

We highlight the inherent modularity of OctopOS, emphasizing this attribute as a key characteristic that makes our device scalable and suitable for integrating security features during the lower-level stages of hardware development, rather than as add-ons.

CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-based approach using automatic segmentation for esophageal tumor

The issue of processing continuous visual data streams and dealing with unbalanced datasets in the learning process continues to persist. Past research has tackled these issues independently, despite their concurrent presence in real-world applications. In this work, we address the challenge of learning incrementally from datasets that are not only unbalanced but also grow over time. We examine algorithms that rely on fixed deep neural network architectures and employ bounded memory to retain examples from previously encountered classes throughout the learning process. Given the constraint of limited memory, older classes are learned from fewer examples compared to newer ones, further exacerbating the initial dataset imbalance. Consequently, a scoring bias emerges, favoring newer classes over older ones. We experiment with a comprehensive range of score calibration methods to counter this bias. Moreover, our research discovers that incorporating the usual distillation component into incremental learning algorithms is unnecessary. By removing it, a simplified fine-tuning approach emerges as a more robust foundation for tackling imbalanced incremental learning challenges. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants who collaborate using identical data attributes, while in the latter, entities with overlapping sample IDs collaborate using different features. Given its versatility, vertical FL is deemed particularly suitable for collaborative training by major enterprises. Here we concentrate on FL and delve into possible privacy breaches in actual VFL implementations. Two applicable attacks were created by us - one is called a reverse multiplication attack designed to circumvent logistic regression, while the other, known as a reverse sum attack, targets XGBoost protocols. Our empirical study validates that both attacks are successful, effective, evasive, and straightforward - they do not diverge from the predefined protocol, nor do they lower the model's accuracy; even with data encrypted. Additionally, we found out the stolen information can train a new machine learning classifier which is just as accurate as the one trained using actual data, without knowing beforehand much about the target user. Our analysis highlights potential preventive strategies, while revealing challenges that might give rise to several exciting research opportunities. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion. Consequently, market design and operational storage management require more sophisticated approaches that consider risk preferences, perhaps through the implementation of price volatility metrics as additional market clearing objectives. This could enhance the performance of storage units and mitigate the negative effects of low probability, high impact events. Ultimately, our research underscores the critical need for storage units to be designed with price volatility in mind, through the use of techniques such as risk neutral pricing or robust optimization. This work also highlights the importance of further research on risk management in electricity markets with high penetrations of storage and renewable energy sources. This research is a precursor to an ongoing project that employs techniques such as robust optimization and implicit pricing to address storage units' risk aversion. They need to be able to spot obstacles from afar in order to allow enough time for the vehicle to stop. Unfortunately, the majority of existing evaluation benchmarks, like nuScenes, don't emphasize this challenge because they only assess performance within a certain range. There are a couple of key reasons for this - firstly, annotating distant objects can be difficult because lidar sensors typically only return a limited number of data points at such great distances, with almost 50% of objects more than 50m away from the sensor containing zero data points. Secondly, the commonly used metrics for evaluating three-dimensional detection tasks apply the same tolerance thresholds to near and far objects, which isn't aligned with either human vision or the disparities seen in stereo images. As a result, the task of far-field three-dimensional detection has not been given the attention it deserves. The model allows one species to colonize nearest-neighbor sites, while another species can settle at any distance but is less successful in doing so. The model includes external noise, which can lead to random species swaps in the lattice. The combination of these dynamics results in various species competition outcomes, including the exclusion of one species, distinct population coexistence, or bistable coexistence dependent on the starting population ratio. The model shows that an abrupt transition occurs as immigration intensity surpasses a critical point, causing the irreversible decline of the species with shorter dispersal range due to a cusp catastrophe leading to half loop dynamics. The dynamics of the model are examined through a disaster event, and the occurrence of a hysteresis loop is observed. The model's analysis is supported by numerical simulations and graphical representations. The model's asymmetrical design provides a basic framework for understanding the complex interactions of species with varying dispersal ranges and competitive abilities. The model's principles can be applied to explore the dynamics of cities, rivers, and ocean currents that influence species migration. This knowledge eventually spread to Indonesia through Islamic cultural influences. Indonesian sundials developed as a reflection of local advancements in astronomy, technology, art, and architecture, with historical examples warranting detailed documentation and study, though often overlooked in existing literature. To collect necessary spatial and temporal information on these sundials, a citizen science initiative could be implemented, addressing research inquiries while promoting science education among the general public. This concept has been proposed as a framework, referred to as the Suryakala-Nusantara program, to explore sundials through citizen science methods. The program's design includes six key components: raising awareness, establishing a database, constructing sundials, conducting observations, organizing workshops, and providing educational materials. By sharing the program's approach, it is hoped that it will inspire similar citizen science projects in other regions with rich sundial histories. Additionally, discussions are being initiated on potential collaborations and data-sharing arrangements among participating teams. The program's outcomes are presented in a standardized digital format, complete with the results of measurements taken from 13 Indonesian sundials, although further analysis is still pending. Continuous support and funding are necessary to maintain and expand the database, making it an apt example for democratizing access to cultural heritage artifacts through citizen science methods. The program's success has also highlighted the importance of preserving historical sundials and promoting science

Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. This approach involves introducing an extra dimension to account for uncertainty and proposes an innovative energy-based objective function to unify both classification tasks and uncertainty modeling. Furthermore, theoretical analysis reveals that optimizing this function effectively captures the marginal data distribution in the uncertainty dimension. Our experiments demonstrate that Energy-based Open-World Softmax, this proposed method, outperforms current best practices in enhancing confidence calibration. This model also achieves a notable increase in uncertainty visibility on complex datasets, indicating that EOW-Softmax effectively models both certain and uncertain predictions accurately. As a result, EOW-Softmax is ideally suited for critical applications where both reliable classification and uncertainty assessment are crucial. During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. Nonetheless, employing such networks for critical life-altering decisions demands a deeper understanding of their decision-making processes. Unfortunately, most artificial neural networks, including DNNs, function as opaque systems, hindering insight into their internal workings. Although some research has initiated the quest to illuminate their behavior, the field of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) remains underdeveloped. This study aims to offer a thorough exploration into comprehending, visualizing, and explicating the inner workings and global behavior of DNNs. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel masks for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results using multiple Convolutional Neural Network configurations. 
Our ultimate goal is to develop a general-purpose, real-time detection system capable of recognizing multiple weather conditions, and our findings serve as a foundation for achieving this goal.

This approach involves two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian, whose gradual transformation from driver to problem form allows researchers to find the target ground state. Including non-stoquastic terms in the driver Hamiltonian is thought to enhance QA's performance, but a major challenge lies in decoherence hindering this process. Surprisingly, we demonstrate that including anti-ferromagnetic interactions within the Hamiltonian results in catastrophic QA failure even with infinitely long annealing periods, a consequence stemming from block-diagonalization and symmetry-related crossing during QA. Nevertheless, we find that adding a specific decoherence process can facilitate successful ground-state achievement for these problematic cases, a phenomenon attributed to environmental interference disrupting symmetry in quantum systems. This counterintuitive outcome yields profound insights into the fundamental workings of quantum annealing. Moreover, our findings suggest that environmental noise might be exploited to bypass stoquasticity constraints in practical applications. Ultimately, our research highlights the intricate interplay between symmetry, quantum interference, and environmental noise in quantum annealing, underscoring the necessity of considering these factors in the design of efficient QA algorithms.

considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, even the best-performing model (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) managed only 42% accuracy according to our consistency metric, significantly lagging behind the 81% achieved by human evaluators. In a bid to fuel further NLP innovations, we publicly release our dataset, along with comprehensive evaluations involving fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot scenarios. a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms. This paper also includes a node sampling policy that generates approximately unbiased gradient estimates at a lower communication cost. A numerical study is conducted to validate the algorithm's performance. The code is available at https://github.com/chenfei777/Adaptive-RW. amplified over the past century through the vast growth of scientific literature. However, despite employing metrics such as citation counts and impact factors, it remains unclear how a discipline's knowledge amount correlates with productivity, specifically how the value of new knowledge varies with each new advancement. To address this question, researchers compiled 185 million articles spanning 19 disciplines and analyzed the citation networks between authors, essentially mapping the evolution of scientific knowledge within each area. Using both structured and unstructured entropies to analyze the resulting data, they devised the Quantitative Index of Knowledge (KQI), which measures knowledge amount as a disorder difference created by increasing order within the scientific literature. Subsequently, they discovered that the growth of new literature accelerates the growth of new knowledge, but there is an evident slowdown before this threshold. Furthermore, some disciplines, like cardiology, have surpassed this limit and are therefore considered knowledge-intensive. Moreover, the acceleration of new knowledge also leads to an increase in potential useful combinations, but this does not yet translate to an analogous acceleration in productivity, as seen in the slowdown in publication speed across all disciplines. The findings provide actionable insights that can guide funding priorities and research agendas, also highlighting the necessity to differentiate between early and late-stage disciplines in both basic research and technological innovation. The growth patterns of new knowledge and literature have substantial implications for the development of expert systems, innovative teams, and successful collaboration. The innovative hardware-induced data corruption detection and prevention strategy proposes using the reliable hardware characteristics to train a supervisor neural network, which in turn enhances the reliability of a computer vision system that learns from an unsound hardware environment. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in upgrading the quality of low-dose images without needing matched high-dose images as reference data.
